title: Ranges and Weights
focus: Precompute the range. Keep the window honest. Let the cheapest edge go first.

cards.title: Prefix Sum
cards.trigger: Repeated range queries, or 'count subarrays summing to k' on an array that may contain negatives.
cards.recall: Write the prefix-plus-hashmap counter from memory. Then answer the question everyone gets wrong: why must the map start with `{0: 1}`?
useWhen: Many range-sum queries on a static array
Count subarrays with an exact sum, including negatives
Subarray with equal counts of two symbols, map them to +1 and -1
Range updates offline, use the difference array
2D region sums, the same idea with inclusion and exclusion
template: # Count subarrays summing to k. Works with negatives; sliding window does not.
# Difference array: O(1) range add, one final sweep
# then prefix-sum diff to get the final array
keyInsights: `{0: 1}` accounts for subarrays that start at index 0. Without it you miss every prefix that itself equals k
Count before you record, or an element of value 0 counts itself
The moment the array has negatives, sliding window is dead and prefix-plus-map is the only linear answer
cards.trap: 'Now do it for a 2D matrix.' Build row prefixes, then sweep every pair of columns and run the 1D algorithm. O(cols^2 * rows), and knowing that shape is the point.

cards.title: Monotonic Deque
cards.trigger: Sliding window maximum or minimum, where the window moves and you must not rescan it.
cards.recall: Write the sliding window maximum from memory. Then answer: why do you store indices instead of values, and what are the two separate eviction rules?
useWhen: Max or min of every window of size k
Shortest subarray with sum at least k, on prefix sums
Constrained DP where the transition is a max over a moving range
Jump games with a bounded jump length
Stock spans and temperature spans over a window
template: dq = deque()          # indices, values strictly decreasing
# 1. evict from the BACK anything this value dominates
# 2. evict from the FRONT anything that fell out of the window
out.append(nums[dq[0]])   # front is always the max
keyInsights: Indices, because the front eviction is a position test and you cannot test a value for staleness
Two evictions with different reasons: back for dominance, front for expiry. Mixing them up is the usual bug
Amortised O(n) because every index is appended once and popped at most once. Say 'amortised' out loud
cards.trap: 'Why not a heap?' A heap gives O(n log k) and needs lazy deletion for stale entries. The deque is O(n). Being able to compare the two is the real answer.

cards.title: Lowest Common Ancestor
cards.trigger: Two nodes, and you need the deepest node that has both in its subtree.
cards.recall: Write the recursive LCA from memory. Then answer the subtle part: when both recursive calls return non-null, why is the current node necessarily the answer?
useWhen: Lowest common ancestor in a binary tree or a BST
Distance between two nodes, depth(a) + depth(b) - 2 * depth(lca)
Path between two nodes in a tree
Any 'deepest node covering both' phrasing
Repeated queries, which pushes you to binary lifting
template: # Binary tree, assumes both nodes exist
if not node or node is p or node is q:
return node          # p and q split here -> this is the LCA
return left or right     # both are on one side, pass it up
# BST: no recursion needed, just walk until the values straddle
if p.val < node.val and q.val < node.val:   node = node.left
elif p.val > node.val and q.val > node.val: node = node.right
dist = depth(p) + depth(q) - 2 * depth(lca(root, p, q))

problem.name: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree

keyInsights: Both sides non-null means one target is left and the other is right, so nothing deeper can contain both
The base case returns the node itself, which is what makes an ancestor-of-itself case work
The BST version is O(h) and needs no recursion. If they say BST and you write the general version, you missed the point
cards.trap: 'The nodes might not exist in the tree.' The clean version returns a wrong answer. You need to count matches found and verify both, and they will ask.

cards.title: Two-Sequence DP
patterns: Mismatch: max of the two skips
cards.trigger: Two sequences compared against each other, and the answer is an alignment.
cards.recall: Say what `dp[i][j]` means over the two prefixes, then write both branches of the recurrence before revealing.
useWhen: Longest common subsequence or substring
Edit distance and its weighted variants
Is one string a subsequence of another, counted
Diff and merge algorithms
Shortest common supersequence, which is m + n - lcs
template: # dp[i][j] = LCS of a[:i] and b[:j]
# Rolled to two rows when you do not need to reconstruct
# ... fill cur from prev, then prev, cur = cur, prev
# mismatch resets to 0, and the answer is the running max, not dp[m][n]
keyInsights: 1-indexed dp with a zero row and column removes every boundary special case. Always pad
Subsequence versus substring changes the mismatch branch from `max` to `0`, and moves where the answer lives
Rolling to two rows is free. Rolling to one row needs a saved diagonal, and that is where people break it
cards.trap: 'Reconstruct the actual subsequence, not just the length.' You need the full table and a backward walk. If you rolled to two rows you cannot, and you must say so.

cards.title: Dijkstra's Algorithm
cards.trigger: Shortest path with non-negative weights. If weights are all equal, use BFS instead.
cards.recall: Write Dijkstra from memory including the stale-entry skip. Then answer: why is the first time you pop a node also the last time you need to look at it, and why does that argument collapse with a negative edge?
useWhen: Single-source shortest path, weighted, non-negative
Network delay, minimum travel cost, cheapest route
Path of maximum probability, negate the log
Grid with per-cell entry cost
Minimax path, swim in rising water, by changing the relax rule
template: continue                      # stale entry, already settled better
# Minimax variant: replace nd = d + w with nd = max(d, w)
# and the same skeleton solves 'minimise the largest edge on the path'
keyInsights: The stale skip replaces decrease-key. Without it you re-expand nodes and the complexity argument falls apart
First pop is final because every edge is non-negative, so no later path can be shorter. That sentence is the proof
Swap `+` for `max` and you get bottleneck paths. Same heap, same skeleton, different relax
cards.trap: 'One edge has weight -1.' Dijkstra silently returns a wrong answer rather than failing. Bellman-Ford is the fix, and recognising the failure is the test.
